'''Robert Woodhouse''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (28 April 1773{{snd}}23 December 1827) was a British mathematician and astronomer.

==Biography==
===Early life and education===
Robert Woodhouse was born on 28 April 1773 in [[Norwich]], [[Norfolk]], the son of Robert Woodhouse, [[Cloth merchant|linen draper]], and Judith Alderson, the daughter of a [[Unitarianism|Unitarian]] minister from [[Lowestoft]].<ref name="Mac" /> Robert junior was baptised at [[St George's Church, Colegate, Norwich]], on 19 May, 1773.<ref>Robert Woodhouse in "the Norfolk, England, Transcripts of Church of England Baptism, Marriage and Burial Registers, 1600–1935, ''FamilySearch'' ([https://search.ancestry.co.uk/cgi-bin/sse.dll?viewrecord=1&r=5538&db=NorfolkBishops&indiv=try&h=2660897 Robert Woodhouse]). Citing ''Archdeacon Transcripts 1600–1812''. {{registration required}}</ref> A younger son, John Thomas Woodhouse, was born in 1780. The brothers were educated at the [[Paston School]] in [[North Walsham]], {{convert|24|km}} north of Norwich.<ref name="Mac">{{cite web |last1=O'Connor |first1=John J. |last2=Robertson |first2=Edmund F. |title=Robert Woodhouse |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Woodhouse/ |website=MacTutor |publisher=University of St Andrews |access-date=24 September 2021 |date=2005}}</ref>

In May 1790 Woodhouse was admitted to [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge|Gonville and Caius College]], [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]],<ref name="Mac" /> the college where Paston pupils were traditionally sent.<ref name="Paston">{{cite web |title=The History of Paston College |url=https://www.paston.ac.uk/our-college/the-history-of-paston-college/ |publisher=[[Paston College]] |access-date=24 September 2021}}</ref><!-- (BA 1795) --> In 1795 he graduated as the [[Senior Wrangler]] (ranked first among the mathematics undergraduates at the university), and took the First [[Smith's Prize]].<ref name="Mac" /> He obtained his [[Master's degree]] at Cambridge in 1798.<ref name="Cambridge" />

===Marriage and career at Cambridge===
[[File:Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge Wellcome M0012088.jpg|thumb|[[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]] by [[David Loggan]] (1688)]]
[[File:Robert Woodhouse Anal Calc.png|thumb|The frontispiece of Woodhouse's ''Principles of Analytical Calculation'' (1803)]]
Woodhouse was a [[fellow]] of the college from 1798 to 1823,{{refn|1=Woodhouse's younger brother John was also a fellow at the college.{{sfn|Becher|2004}}|group=note}} after which he resigned so as to be able to marry Harriet, the daughter of William Wilkin, a Norwich architect.<ref name="Mac" /><ref name="Cambridge">{{acad |id=WDHS790R |name=Robert Woodhouse |volume= |year= |ref= |access-date=24 September 2021 |hide errors=}}</ref> They were married on 20 February 1823; the marriage produced a son, also named Robert.<ref name="Mac" /><ref name="Cambridge" /> Harriet Woodhouse died at Cambridge on 31 March 1826.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biographies T - Z |url=https://www.ast.cam.ac.uk/about/history/biographies.t.-.z |publisher=[[Institute of Astronomy, Cambridge]] |access-date=24 September 2021 |archive-date=22 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190722080141/https://www.ast.cam.ac.uk/about/history/biographies.t.-.z |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Woodhouse was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] on 16 December 1802.<ref name="RSoc">{{cite web |title=Record: Woodhouse; Robert (1773–1827) |url=https://catalogues.royalsociety.org/CalmView/Record.aspx?src=CalmView.Persons&id=NA8096&pos=1 |publisher=[[The Royal Society]] |access-date=24 September 2021}}</ref> His earliest work, entitled the ''Principles of Analytical Calculation'', was published at Cambridge in 1803.{{sfn|Rouse Ball|1912|p=440}} In this he explained the [[differential notation]] and strongly pressed the employment of it; but he severely criticised the methods used by continental writers, and their constant assumption of non-evident principles.{{sfn|Becher|1980|pp=389{{ndash}}400}}

In 1809 Woodhouse published a textbook covering [[trigonometry|planar trigonometry]] and [[spherical trigonometry]] and the next year a historical [[treatise]] on the [[calculus of variations]] and [[isoperimetry|isoperimetrical problems]]. He next produced an [[astronomy]]; of which the first book (usually bound in two volumes), on practical and descriptive astronomy, was issued in 1812, and the second book, containing an account of the treatment of physical astronomy by [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] and other continental writers, was issued in 1818.{{sfn|Rouse Ball|1912|p=440}}

Woodhouse became the [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics]] in 1820, but the small income caused him to resign the professorship in 1822 and instead accept the better paid post as the [[Plumian Professor of Astronomy and Experimental Philosophy|Plumian professor]] in the university.<ref name="Mac" />{{sfn|Guicciardini|1989|p=126}} As Plumian Professor he was responsible for installing and adjusting the transit instruments and clocks at the [[Cambridge Observatory]].{{sfn|Woodhouse|1825|pp=418{{ndash}}428}}

Woodhouse did not exercise much influence on the majority of his contemporaries, and the movement might have died away for the time being if it had not been for the advocacy of [[George Peacock (mathematician)|George Peacock]], [[Charles Babbage]], and [[John Herschel]], who formed the [[Analytical Society]], with the object of advocating the general use in the university of analytical methods and of the differential notation.{{sfn|Rouse Ball|1912|pp=440{{ndash}}441}} Woodhouse was the first director of the newly built [[Cambridge Observatory|observatory at Cambridge]], a post he held until his death in 1827.<ref name="Mac" />

On his death in Cambridge he was buried in [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge|Caius College]] chapel.<ref name="RSoc" />
